title: Chapter 3 Mastery Quiz: Subcortical Systems & The Cerebral Cortex
description: Test your mastery of the thalamus, hypothalamus, amygdala, hippocampus, basal ganglia motor loops, and the cerebral lobes.

questions.question: Which specific thalamic nucleus receives retinal inputs and projects visual information to the primary visual cortex (V1)?
questions.explanation: The LGN is the primary thalamic relay station for visual processing.

questions.question: Which thalamic nucleus relays auditory information from the brainstem to the primary auditory cortex?
questions.explanation: The MGN (Medial = Music/Auditory) relays auditory signals to the primary auditory cortex.

questions.question: The hypothalamus regulates the endocrine system primarily by controlling secretions from which gland?

options.text: Thyroid gland directly via cranial nerves

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus regulates the anterior pituitary via hypophyseal portal hormones and posterior pituitary via direct neurosecretion.

questions.question: Stimulation of the Lateral Hypothalamus (LH) in rodents triggers which immediate behavior?

options.text: Immediate entry into deep REM sleep
Suppression of heart rate and respiration

questions.explanation: The lateral hypothalamus functions as a hunger center; stimulating it induces feeding.

questions.question: In Pavlovian fear conditioning, an auditory tone paired with an aversive shock converges in which amygdalar region?
questions.explanation: The basolateral amygdala is the primary sensory convergence site where associative fear conditioning occurs.

questions.question: Klüver-Bucy syndrome, resulting from bilateral anterior temporal lobe and amygdala lesions, is characterized by:

options.text: Profound loss of fear, hyperorality, visual agnosia, and hypersexuality
Extreme aggression, intense panic attacks, and insomnia
Rigid muscle paralysis and resting pill-rolling tremors
Complete inability to comprehend spoken words

questions.explanation: Klüver-Bucy syndrome involves loss of fear reactivity (tameness), hyperorality, psychic blindness, and hypersexuality.

questions.question: Patient H.M. experienced severe anterograde amnesia following surgical removal of which bilateral structures?

options.text: Medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampi

questions.explanation: H.M. underwent bilateral medial temporal lobe resection to treat epilepsy, losing the hippocampi and adjacent entorhinal/parahippocampal cortices.

questions.question: What critical distinction in human memory systems was proven by Patient H.M.'s preserved performance on the mirror-tracing task?

options.text: Procedural motor memory does not depend on the hippocampus, while conscious episodic memory does
All memories are stored permanently in the spinal cord
Visual memories bypass the brainstem entirely
Short-term working memory lasts up to three hours

questions.explanation: H.M. mastered motor skills without conscious recall, demonstrating a fundamental dissociation between declarative and non-declarative memory.

questions.question: The Striatum is anatomically comprised of which two subcortical structures?
questions.explanation: The striatum is formed by the caudate nucleus and the putamen, which receive cortical glutamatergic inputs.

questions.question: In the basal ganglia direct pathway, dopamine binds to which type of receptor in the striatum to facilitate movement?
questions.explanation: Dopamine excites direct pathway medium spiny neurons via Gs-coupled D1 dopamine receptors, promoting movement initiation.

questions.question: What is the primary neuropathology of Parkinson's disease?

options.text: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta
Loss of striatal GABAergic neurons in the indirect pathway
Atrophy of the primary somatosensory cortex

questions.explanation: Loss of neuromelanin-containing dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta reduces striatal dopamine, causing Parkinsonism.

questions.question: Which genetic mutation is responsible for Huntington's disease?

options.text: An expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the Huntingtin (HTT) gene
Duplication of the amyloid precursor protein gene
Inactivation of the survival motor neuron 1 gene

questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion disorder that causes striatal medium spiny neuron degeneration.

questions.question: How many histological layers typically compose the mammalian Neocortex?
questions.explanation: The neocortex is characterized by its distinct 6-layered cytoarchitectonic structure.

questions.question: Where is the Primary Motor Cortex located in the human brain?

options.text: Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
Calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe

questions.explanation: The primary motor cortex (Brodmann Area 4) sits on the precentral gyrus immediately anterior to the central sulcus.

questions.question: A stroke affecting Broca's Area in the left hemisphere characteristically results in:

options.text: Expressive aphasia: non-fluent, halting speech with relatively preserved comprehension
Fluent word salad speech with complete inability to understand words
Complete visual blindness in both visual fields
Severe resting tremor of both hands

questions.explanation: Broca's aphasia impairs motor speech production, leading to telegraphic, non-fluent speech while comprehension remains intact.

questions.question: A stroke affecting Wernicke's Area in the left temporal lobe produces:

options.text: Receptive aphasia: fluent, grammatically normal speech that lacks semantic meaning, accompanied by poor comprehension
Severe stuttering and physical inability to move the vocal cords
Hemispatial neglect of the left half of visual space
Complete paralysis of the right arm

questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia impairs language comprehension, resulting in fluent, effortless, but semantically nonsensical speech.

questions.question: Damage to the right posterior parietal cortex frequently results in which neuropsychological syndrome?

options.text: Hemispatial neglect (ignoring stimuli in the contralateral left visual and physical space)
Retrograde amnesia for events before age ten

questions.explanation: Right parietal lesions cause hemispatial neglect, where patients fail to notice, respond, or orient to items in their left environment.

questions.question: What primary psychological function was severely disrupted in Phineas Gage following iron rod trauma to his ventromedial prefrontal cortex?

options.text: Social judgment, emotional regulation, and impulse inhibition
Motor speech articulation and grammatical parsing
Ability to calculate arithmetic sums and recite poetry

questions.explanation: Gage retained intellectual and motor capacity, but suffered profound deficits in personality, social appropriateness, and impulse control.

questions.question: Where is the Primary Visual Cortex (Striate Cortex / V1) located?

options.text: Occipital lobe along the banks of the calcarine sulcus
Inferior surface of the temporal lobe
Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe

questions.explanation: Primary visual cortex (Brodmann Area 17) is buried inside the calcarine fissure of the occipital lobe.

questions.question: The Fusiform Face Area (FFA), specialized for recognizing human faces, is situated in which region?
questions.explanation: The FFA is located on the lateral fusiform gyrus within the ventral temporal stream; lesions cause prosopagnosia.

questions.question: What happens when the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in the indirect pathway is selectively destroyed (e.g., by lacunar stroke)?

options.text: Hemiballismus: wild, violent flinging movements of the contralateral limbs
Total paralysis of all facial expressions
Immediate coma and loss of brainstem reflexes
Loss of taste sensation on the anterior tongue

questions.explanation: STN lesions remove excitation to GPi/SNr, causing catastrophic disinhibition of the motor thalamus and violent flinging limb movements.

questions.question: Which neocortical layer contains the massive pyramidal cell bodies that send long-distance efferent motor axons into the corticospinal tract?
questions.explanation: Layer V houses giant Betz pyramidal cells that project motor commands down through the brainstem and spinal cord.
